questions.title: Known kilometre-wide asteroids that come close to Earth
questions.unitLabel: near-Earth asteroids ~1 km or larger known on 1 January
questions.hint: In 1998 the US Congress told NASA to find 90% of the near-Earth asteroids big enough to cause a global catastrophe; there are only so many of them.
questions.explanation: It rose to 879 in 2024, from 299 in 2000. The Spaceguard surveys found them fast, then discoveries slowed to a handful a year because almost all of them had been found. Size is judged from brightness, so ‘about 1 km’ is approximate.

source.attribution: NASA/JPL-Caltech, Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS)

questions.title: Pieces of tracked space debris orbiting Earth
questions.unitLabel: catalogued debris fragments in orbit at year end
questions.hint: Fragments are created by explosions, collisions and weapons tests, and removed only when air drag pulls them down, which is strongest when the Sun is most active.
questions.explanation: It rose to 11,456 in 2012, from 5,458 in 2000. China’s 2007 anti-satellite test and the 2009 collision of the Iridium 33 and Cosmos 2251 satellites made the jumps. Only fragments big enough to be tracked (roughly 10 cm and up) count, from astronomer Jonathan McDowell’s General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects.

source.attribution: Jonathan McDowell, General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects (GCAT)

questions.title: Share of Nobel science laureates working in the US
questions.unitLabel: % of physics, chemistry and medicine laureates with a US affiliation, by decade
questions.hint: European universities ruled early science; then came war, refugees, and enormous postwar research budgets.
questions.explanation: It went from 3% in 1900 to a high of 72% in 1990, then ended at 58% in 2020. Refugee scientists and wartime and postwar federal research money flipped the balance from the 1940s. Counted by where laureates worked when they won, not nationality. Physics, chemistry and medicine only; each point is a decade of prizes, and 2020 covers 2020-2026 only.

questions.title: Rocket launches into orbit worldwide
questions.unitLabel: orbital launch attempts a year, including failures
questions.hint: Launches follow the space race, government budgets, and lately the cost of reusable rockets and satellite networks.
questions.explanation: It rose to 114 in 2020, from 38 in 1960. Counted by astronomer Jonathan McDowell from his General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects.

source.attribution: Jonathan McDowell, General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects (GCAT)

questions.title: Arctic sea ice in September (the yearly low point)
questions.hint: Satellites have mapped the floating ice on the Arctic Ocean since 1979; warmer air and water, winds and the thinning of old multi-year ice decide how much survives the summer.
questions.explanation: It went from 6.69 M km² in 1997 to a low of 3.57 M km² in 2012, then ended at 4.35 M km² in 2024. The ice plunged in 2007 and hit a record low in 2012; since then it has hovered around 4-5 million km² without a new record. From the NSIDC Sea Ice Index, measured by satellite.

source.attribution: National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), Sea Ice Index
